meta.title: Who originally recorded "Pass the Dutchie"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Musical Youth didn't originate it. The song was first recorded in 1981 by the Mighty Diamonds as "Pass the Kouchie" for Jamaica's Music Works label.
meta.ogDescription: Not a Musical Youth original: the Mighty Diamonds cut it in 1981 as "Pass the Kouchie", produced by Gussie Clarke and banned from Jamaican radio.

answer.label: Not a Musical Youth original — a 1981 Mighty Diamonds single, “Pass the Kouchie”
answer.originalArtistDates: Formed 1969, Trenchtown, Kingston · Jamaican roots reggae vocal trio
answer.sourceLine: Musical Youth’s 1982 record is so completely theirs in memory that most people assume they made it up. They didn’t: the song was first recorded in 1981 by the Mighty Diamonds as “Pass the Kouchie”, produced by Augustus “Gussie” Clarke for the Music Works label and carried on the album Changes. The composition credits run to Diamonds members Fitzroy “Bunny” Simpson and Lloyd “Judge” Ferguson alongside Jackie Mittoo, whose rocksteady instrumental “Full Up” supplies the rhythm. The Jamaican original was condemned by Prime Minister Edward Seaga and banned from national radio — and in 2012 the English High Court held that the British hit shared the same copyright as the Jamaican one.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: Music Works
original.released: Issued in Jamaica in 1981 as “Pass the Kouchie” by the Mighty Diamonds — a Music Works single (it circulated on 10″ and 12″ pressings) and a track on the Gussie Clarke–produced album Changes.
original.charted: No international chart placing. It was condemned by Jamaican Prime Minister Edward Seaga and banned from national radio, yet became a top seller in Jamaican record shops.
original.writer: The Mighty Diamonds (adapted from Leroy Sibbles' 1968 instrumental 'Full Up')
original.cover: Musical Youth’s rewritten version, “Pass the Dutchie”, was released by MCA Records on 10 September 1982. It went to No. 1 in the UK and reached No. 10 on the US Billboard Hot 100 in February 1983.

trail: Wikipedia’s entry on “Pass the Kouchie” ↗ records the 1981 Mighty Diamonds original, the Seaga condemnation and the Jamaican radio ban.
The Mighty Diamonds’ own band entry ↗ places the song on Changes (1981), released by Music Works and produced by Gussie Clarke.

The 2012 English High Court judgment in Seaton & Ors v Seddon & Ors ↗, decided by Mr Justice Roth on 23 March 2012, treats “Pass the Dutchie” as an adaptation of “Pass the Kouchie” and traces the underlying music to Jackie Mittoo’s “Full Up”.
MusicBrainz’s work entry ↗ lists “Pass the Dutchie” as an alias of the same composition and credits seven writers, among them Simpson, Ferguson, Mittoo, Leroy Sibbles and U Brown.

authors.name: The Mighty Diamonds
authors.heading: Who actually cut it first
authors.metaLine: Roots reggae vocal trio, formed 1969, Trenchtown, Kingston
authors.bio: Donald “Tabby” Shaw sang lead, with Fitzroy “Bunny” Simpson and Lloyd “Judge” Ferguson in harmony — a Motown-shaped vocal group working in the roots idiom, and by the mid-1970s one of the most respected acts in Jamaica on the strength of Right Time. “Pass the Kouchie” arrived in 1981 on Gussie Clarke’s Music Works label and promptly got them denounced by the Prime Minister and banned from national radio, which did nothing to slow it in the record shops. Simpson and Ferguson are two of the three credited writers of the composition. Shaw was killed in a drive-by shooting in March 2022; Simpson died days later.

authors.name: Musical Youth
authors.heading: The version everybody knows
authors.metaLine: British reggae group, formed 1979, Birmingham, England
authors.bio: Two pairs of brothers — Kelvin and Michael Grant, Frederick “Junior” and Patrick Waite — assembled by their fathers while still at Duddeston Manor School in Birmingham. Their MCA single went to No. 1 in the UK and No. 10 in the US, sold in the millions, and its Don Letts–directed video became the first by a black act to air on MTV. None of that is diminished by the chronology: it is a superb record made by children who were handed someone else’s song and a set of rewritten words, and the only error in the popular memory is the word “original”.

misattribution.heading: Right record, wrong origin story
misattribution.intro: Nobody disputes that Musical Youth made the hit. What gets lost is that they were covering a Jamaican single that was barely a year old at the time — and that a court eventually said so in as many words.

items.why: Their MCA single reached No. 1 in the UK and No. 10 in the US, and its MTV airplay made it one of the most-seen reggae records of the decade. It is a cover with rewritten lyrics, not an original.
Released as “Pass the Kouchie” on Gussie Clarke’s Music Works label and included on the album Changes. Banned from Jamaican national radio after Prime Minister Edward Seaga condemned it.

items.who: Fitzroy “Bunny” Simpson, Lloyd “Judge” Ferguson and Jackie Mittoo
items.why: Two Mighty Diamonds plus the rocksteady keyboardist whose instrumental “Full Up” underpins the rhythm. MusicBrainz’s entry for the composition adds Leroy Sibbles, U Brown, Robbie Lyn and “Deadly” Headley Bennett to the credit list.

In Seaton & Ors v Seddon & Ors, Mr Justice Roth treated “Pass the Dutchie” as an adaptation sharing the copyright of “Pass the Kouchie”; the former Musical Youth members’ claim against their old solicitors was dismissed.

misattribution.truthLine: First recorded by the Mighty Diamonds in 1981, as “Pass the Kouchie”.

context.heading: Why the cover swallowed the original
lead: The interesting thing here is that the eclipse was engineered. The Mighty Diamonds’ record was about Rastafarian cannabis use and said so plainly; a “kouchie” is the pipe. When the song was rebuilt for the British market in 1982, the record company had the drug references taken out — the title became “dutchie”, a patois word for a Dutch oven, and the song was reframed around food. A record designed for radio replaced a record that had been banned from it. Wikipedia notes the further irony that “dutchie” itself later drifted into cannabis slang anyway.

The other reason is arithmetic of reach. The Jamaican original was a Music Works pressing in a national market with the state broadcaster closed to it; the adaptation had MCA, a Don Letts video and MTV in its first year of existence. Wikipedia records that the British version also folded in U Brown’s “Gimme the Music”, so what most listeners hear as one catchy novelty is in fact several Jamaican records stacked on top of Jackie Mittoo’s rhythm.
detailsBody: 1968 — the rocksteady instrumental “Full Up” is cut in Kingston; the 2012 High Court judgment attributes the music to Jackie Mittoo, and Wikipedia, citing musicologist George Lipsitz, credits Leroy Sibbles. Both men appear on the composition’s writer list.
1981 — the Mighty Diamonds record “Pass the Kouchie” for Augustus “Gussie” Clarke’s Music Works label; it appears on the album Changes.
1981 — Prime Minister Edward Seaga condemns the record and it is banned from Jamaican national radio. It sells heavily in record shops regardless.
1982 — Musical Youth record an adaptation in August with the drug references removed. MCA releases “Pass the Dutchie” on 10 September; it tops the UK chart.
February 1983 — the single peaks at No. 10 on the US Billboard Hot 100; the video has already become the first by a black act shown on MTV.

23 March 2012 — in Seaton & Ors v Seddon & Ors, Mr Justice Roth confirms the two songs share the same copyright and dismisses the former band members’ claim against their former solicitors as time-barred.
context.pull: A record made for radio replaced a record that had been banned from it.
